> The primary goal of Experiment 1 is to replicate the associational blocking
effect observed by @beesley2011 in a large-scale online sample, to ensure the
effect is replicable in our laboratory environment before trying to extend the
original findings.

::: {.callout-tip title="Goals"}
In this report, the aims are to:

1. **inform expectations** about the true effect size, from the literature and
   from the feasibility study,
2. **conduct a formal power analysis** of the original index (BI~2~) to estimate
   a sufficient sample size, and evaluate the power of the alternative index
   (BI~3~) at that sample size,
3. **set the rules** for declaring (non-)replication and for the
   group-sequential top-up of the sample if needed.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="90% confidence intervals"}
Because the replication study `fba-allergy-online-02` aims to detect blocking
in a design for which there is a strong theoretical justification of expecting
its direction *a priori*, the study pre-registers and employs a one-sided *t*-test
with the alternative hypothesis of the effect being greater than zero.
Consequently, all effect size estimates presented in this notebook are
accompanied by their **90% confidence intervals** (CIs), not 95% CIs, as the
former align better with the one-sided test.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Set-up"}
```{r}
#| label: replication-pwr-envir
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(tidyverse)
  library(gt)
  library(pwrss)
})

# Search files in relation to the project repository directory, so that the
# code remains renderable no matter where it is called from
REPO <- rprojroot::find_root(rprojroot::has_file("CATLAS.Rproj"))

# Formatting helpers shared by all manuscripts
source(file.path(REPO, "common", "R", "utils-print.R"))

# Tables and helpers of this notebook
source(file.path(REPO, "manuscripts", "forward-blocking-attention-01", "R", "03-replication-power.R"))

# Because the replication aims to detect an effect in the predicted direction
# at the 5% level of significance, alpha for CIs is set at 0.10, i.e., 90% CIs, which
# align with this aim better than the typical 95% CIs.
alpha <- .10
```
:::

# Effect size of blocking

## Prior literature

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Literature-based effect size estimates"}
```{r}
#| label: replication-pwr-literature
# Reported tests of blocking in experiments similar to the one being replicated,
# one row per experiment. The F-test of Le Pelley et al. (2007) has one
# numerator degree of freedom, i.e., it is equivalent to a squared paired t-test
literature <- tibble::tribble(
  ~study,            ~index, ~test, ~statistic, ~n,
  "beesley2011",     "BI2",  "t",   2.74,       26L,
  "lepelley2007",    "BI1",  "F",   7.00,       8L,
  "griffiths2009e1", "BI1",  "t",   2.07,       32L,
  "griffiths2009e3", "BI3",  "t",   5.03,       40L
)

# Cohen's d_z with its CI, and the two-sided p-value of each reported test
lit <-
  literature |>
  standardise_reported_tests(level = 1 - alpha) |>
  split(~ study)

# Raw effect magnitude of Beesley and Le Pelley (2011), with the standard
# deviation implied by their test
x_bar <- 2.03
s <- x_bar * sqrt(lit$beesley2011$n) / lit$beesley2011$t
se <- s / sqrt(lit$beesley2011$n)
ci_low <- x_bar - stats::qt(alpha / 2, lit$beesley2011$df, lower.tail = FALSE) * se
ci_upp <- x_bar + stats::qt(alpha / 2, lit$beesley2011$df, lower.tail = FALSE) * se
```
:::

### @beesley2011

@beesley2011 employed the 2AFC *negation test* [@don2018] to measure blocking
and reported mean blocking index[^1] $\mathbb{E}(BI_2) = +2.03$ across their
sample of *N* = 26 participants. After conducting a one-sample two-sided
*t*-test against the null hypothesis $\mathbb{E}(BI_2) = 0$, they concluded that
the observed difference is significantly different from zero, *t*(25) = 2.74,
*p* = .011.

[^1]: See the [Dependent Variables](01-estimands-estimates.qmd) notebook for
definition of BI~2~ and other blocking indexes used to estimate the effect of
blocking in contingency learning experimental paradigms.

Although the authors do not directly provide estimates of effect variance and
its standardised size, these metrics can be deduced from the information about
the raw effect magnitude and *t*-test results.

Firstly, the effect's standard deviation can be calculated from the test
statistic, raw effect magnitude, and sample size:

$$t = \frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{N}}$$
$$2.74 = \frac{2.03-0}{s/\sqrt{26}}$$
$$s = \frac{2.03\sqrt{26}}{2.74} \approx 3.78$$

Secondly, the standardised effect size, Cohen's *d*~z~ (the mean divided by the
standard deviation,), follows as:

$$d_z = \frac{\bar{X}}{s} = \frac{t}{\sqrt{N}} = \frac{2.74}{\sqrt{26}} \approx 0.54$$

Together, these result in:

- Raw effect magnitude:
  $\bar{X} = `r x_bar` \ `r print_ci(ci_low, ci_upp)`$
- Standardised effect size:
  $d_z = `r print_d(lit$beesley2011$d)` \ `r print_ci(lit$beesley2011$d_low, lit$beesley2011$d_high)`$

### Other studies

To further evaluate the most likely values of the true effect size, one might
look at experiments similar to the one aimed to be replicated. Papers most
similar in their experimental design to @beesley2011 are @lepelley2007 and
@griffiths2009. The former introduced the three-stage design in its current form
to address potential competing explanations such as memory interference, while
the latter extended the design to evaluate to what degree the blocking
effect depends on the presence of the original blocking stimulus in Stage 3
learning.

#### @lepelley2007

@lepelley2007 measured blocking using a BI~1~ type of blocking index, with the
exception that instead of evaluating predictive value of each cue separately,
cue-compounds including either two blocked or two control cues associated with
the same outcome were used. In a total of `r lit$lepelley2007$n` participants,
they observed a statistically significant blocking,
*F*(1, `r lit$lepelley2007$df`) = `r lit$lepelley2007$statistic`,
*p* `r print_p(lit$lepelley2007$p)`, translating to
$d_z = `r print_d(lit$lepelley2007$d)` \ `r print_ci(lit$lepelley2007$d_low, lit$lepelley2007$d_high)`$.

#### @griffiths2009

@griffiths2009 measured blocking of the same structure, i.e., comparing blocked
cues with novel control cues after Stage 3 learning, in their Experiments 1 and
3.[^2]

[^2]: Their Experiment 2, although using 2AFC *negation test* with BI~3~-like
measure of blocking, omits the critical blocked cue vs. novel control cue
comparisons.

In Experiment 1, the effect was measured using BI~1~. Based on data from
`r lit$griffiths2009e1$n` participants, @griffiths2009 observed a statistically
significant blocking effect,
*t*(`r lit$griffiths2009e1$df`) = `r lit$griffiths2009e1$statistic`,
*p* `r print_p(lit$griffiths2009e1$p)`, translating to
$d_z = `r print_d(lit$griffiths2009e1$d)` \ `r print_ci(lit$griffiths2009e1$d_low, lit$griffiths2009e1$d_high)`$.

Most relevantly, Experiment 3 of @griffiths2009 estimates blocking using a 2AFC
*negation test* procedure similar to that used by @beesley2011, employing an
estimate similar to BI~3~ based on two test blocks per participant. Based on
data from `r lit$griffiths2009e3$n` participants, @griffiths2009 observed a
statistically significant blocking effect,
*t*(`r lit$griffiths2009e3$df`) = `r lit$griffiths2009e3$statistic`,
*p* `r print_p(lit$griffiths2009e3$p)`, translating to
$d_z = `r print_d(lit$griffiths2009e3$d)` \ `r print_ci(lit$griffiths2009e3$d_low, lit$griffiths2009e3$d_high)`$.

### Summary

The effect sizes observed in experiments similar to @beesley2011 vary widely.
Two of them come with large uncertainty [@lepelley2007] or a relatively small
effect whose 90% CI sits near zero [@griffiths2009, Exp. 1]. Admittedly,
both used BI~1~ as their measure of blocking, which may be less sensitive to
blocking than BI~2~ or BI~3~. Experiment 3 of @griffiths2009 used a BI~3~-like
index and yielded a relatively large effect, larger than the one observed by
@beesley2011.

| Study | Measure | *d*~z~ [90% CI] |
|:------|:-----|:--------------------|
| ***@beesley2011*** | ***BI~2~*** | ***`r print_d(lit$beesley2011$d)` `r print_ci(lit$beesley2011$d_low, lit$beesley2011$d_high)`*** |
| @lepelley2007 | BI~1~ | `r print_d(lit$lepelley2007$d)` `r print_ci(lit$lepelley2007$d_low, lit$lepelley2007$d_high)` |
| @griffiths2009, Exp. 1 | BI~1~ | `r print_d(lit$griffiths2009e1$d)` `r print_ci(lit$griffiths2009e1$d_low, lit$griffiths2009e1$d_high)` |
| @griffiths2009, Exp. 3 | BI~3~ | `r print_d(lit$griffiths2009e3$d)` `r print_ci(lit$griffiths2009e3$d_low, lit$griffiths2009e3$d_high)` |

## Feasibility study

The second type of evidence considered here for setting a realistic value of the
true effect size for the prospective power analysis comes from the feasibility
study `fba-allergy-online-01`. During it, I ran the three-stage design of
@beesley2011 using the modified allergist task online. Its results are reported
in full in the [Feasibility Study](02-feasibility-study.qmd) notebook. The
analysis was conducted on three analysis data sets with increasingly tighter
exclusion criteria:

1. the **full sample** excluded only participants without sufficient
   experimental data,
2. the **learned set** additionally excluded participants failing the learning
   check, and
3. the **naive set** also excluded participants claiming to know the
   experiment.

For reasons explained below, the learned and naive sets swap their roles for the
replication study.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Feasibility estimates"}
```{r}
#| label: replication-pwr-feasibility
# Pilot estimates and attrition funnel, saved by `02-feasibility-study.qmd`
estimates <- read_output("02-feasibility-estimates.rds", REPO)
funnel <- read_output("02-feasibility-funnel.rds", REPO)

# The original index (BI2 on test block 1) and the alternative index (BI3 over
# all test blocks) in each of the three analysis sets, tested one-sided with
# two-sided 90% CIs
sets <- c(
  full    = "1 \u00b7 Full sample",
  learned = "2 \u00b7 Learned",
  naive   = "3 \u00b7 Naive"
)
stopifnot(
  setequal(as.character(estimates$set), sets),
  nrow(estimates) == 6L,
  all(estimates$alternative == "greater"),
  isTRUE(all.equal(unique(estimates$perc), 1 - alpha))
)

d_bi2 <- purrr::map_dbl(sets, \(s) {
  pick_estimate(estimates, s, "bi_confidence")
})

d_bi3 <- purrr::map_dbl(sets, \(s) {
  pick_estimate(estimates, s, "bi_choice")
})

n_sets <- purrr::map_dbl(sets, \(s) {
  pick_estimate(estimates, s, "bi_confidence", "n")
})

# Every interval must cover no blocking and the effect size of Beesley and
# Le Pelley (2011), as the text says
stopifnot(
  all(estimates$d_low < 0),
  all(estimates$d_high > lit$beesley2011$d)
)

# Point estimates of BI3 as range for text
bi3_range <- print_range(c(d_bi3[["learned"]], d_bi3[["full"]]))
```
:::

::: {.callout-important title="The learned and the naive set swap roles"}
| Set | Exclusions | Feasibility | Replication |
|:--|:----|:--|:--|
| 1 · Full sample | structural only | sensitivity | sensitivity |
| 2 · Learned | structural, learning check | **primary** | sensitivity |
| 3 · Naive | structural, learning check, prior knowledge | sensitivity | **primary** |

The table shows each analysis set used in the feasibility study and planned to
be used in the replication study, together with their role in each analysis. The
naive set leaves out participants who report prior knowledge of similar
experiments, and may thus answer according to what they expect the study to show
rather than according to what they learned. In the feasibility study, the
primary analysis set kept these participants
(*n* = `r n_sets[["learned"]] - n_sets[["naive"]]`).

In `fba-allergy-online-02`, the debriefing question becomes a two-parter (asking
about prior experiments of the same kind, and critically adding a question about
knowing or guessing what the study tested) and the naive set becomes the primary
analysis set.
:::

### Effect size estimates

In the full sample and the learned set, BI~2~ on the first test block yielded
*d*~z~ of `r print_d(d_bi2[["full"]])` and `r print_d(d_bi2[["learned"]])`,
respectively, and BI~3~ over all test blocks `r print_d(d_bi3[["full"]])`
and `r print_d(d_bi3[["learned"]])`. In the naive set, both effect sizes were cut
to about half or less (`r print_d(d_bi2[["naive"]])` for BI~2~,
`r print_d(d_bi3[["naive"]])` for BI~3~). None of the one-sided tests rejected
the null hypothesis of no blocking, and every 90% CI includes both zero and
the original study's estimate *d*~z~ &approx; `r print_d(lit$beesley2011$d)` (see the
table below).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-replication-pwr-feasibility
#| tbl-cap: "Effect size estimates of the feasibility study (`fba-allergy-online-01`) per analysis set."
estimates |>
  prepare_pilot_estimates() |>
  tbl_pilot_estimates(level = 1 - alpha)
```

### Retention

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Retention"}
```{r}
#| label: replication-pwr-retention
retention <- summarise_retention(funnel, "Total")
retention_labels <- summarise_retention(funnel, "LABELS")

# The three steps that removed participants in the pilot
stopifnot(identical(
  retention$step,
  c("Incomplete run", "Insufficient learning", "Prior knowledge")
))
yield <- stats::setNames(
  retention$yield,
  retention$step
)

n_records <- funnel$Total[1L]
n_learned <- funnel$Total[nrow(funnel) - 1L]
n_naive <- funnel$Total[nrow(funnel)]
n_records_labels <- funnel$LABELS[1L]
n_naive_labels <- funnel$LABELS[nrow(funnel)]

# Retention if no run were incomplete
yield_complete <- prod(yield[c("Insufficient learning", "Prior knowledge")])
```
:::

Of the `r print_num_word(n_records, TRUE)` JATOS records of the feasibility
study, `r print_num_word(n_learned, TRUE)`
(`r round(100 * n_learned / n_records)`%)
reached the learned set, and `r print_num_word(n_naive)`
(`r round(100 * n_naive / n_records)`%)
reached the naive set (see the table below).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-replication-pwr-retention
#| tbl-cap: "Participant retention through the exclusion steps of the feasibility study, over all recruitment channels and in the LABELS channel alone."
funnel |>
  prepare_retention() |>
  tbl_retention()
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Assumed retention for the `fba-allergy-online-02` study"}
Following the retention rates observed in the feasibility study, I assume
50% retention for `fba-allergy-online-02`, i.e., that half of the participants
who start the experiment will be included in the naive set, the primary analysis
set of the study. The assumption stems from three observations:

- **Incomplete runs**, because of which
  `r print_n_pct(retention$before[1L] - retention$after[1L], n_records)`
  records were excluded, should become rarer. Both incomplete runs of the LABELS
  channel were lost due to unstable internet connections, which is an issue that
  will be solved in the new experimental code (`catlaslab` issue #9).
- **Without incomplete runs**, the yields of the learning check
  (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * yield[["Insufficient learning"]])`) and of the
  prior-knowledge exclusion
  (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * yield[["Prior knowledge"]])`) multiply to
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * yield_complete)`.
- **In the LABELS channel**, from which `fba-allergy-online-02` recruits,
  `r print_n_pct(n_naive_labels, n_records_labels)` records reached the naive
  set.
:::

## Assumed true effect size

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Effect size scenarios"}
```{r}
#| label: replication-pwr-scenarios
# The three scenarios, rounded to two decimals as in the text: the original
# study, the lower of the two main estimates of the feasibility study (the full
# sample), and its naive set
d_best <- round(lit$beesley2011$d, 2)
d_real <- round(d_bi2[["full"]], 2)
d_worst <- round(d_bi2[["naive"]], 2)

stopifnot(d_bi2[["full"]] <= d_bi2[["learned"]])

# Schäfer & Schwarz (2019) correlation estimates converted to d
r_schafer <- c(0.16, 0.36)
d_schafer <- 2 * r_schafer / sqrt(1 - r_schafer^2)
```
:::

The prospective power analysis below combines the estimate of @beesley2011
with those of the feasibility study into three scenarios:

| Scenario | *d*~z~ | Reason |
|:--|:-:|:---------|
| *Worst* | `r d_worst` | Feasibility study's naive set estimate, an effect size considered to be small [cf. @lovakov2021] |
| *Realistic* | `r d_real` | The lower of the feasibility study's full sample and learned set estimates, an effect size considered to be medium [cf. @lovakov2021] |
| *Best* | `r d_best` | The point estimate of the original study [@beesley2011], an effect size between medium and large [cf. @lovakov2021] |

::: {.callout-important title="Effect size magnitude interpretation"}
The size labels used in this notebook follow the empirically derived benchmarks
of @lovakov2021, who set small, medium and large effects at *d* = 0.15, 0.36 and
0.65, respectively. These serve as only a rough guide here, because of the exact
field they were derived from (social psychology, not learning, experimental or
cognitive psychology), and the fact they describe standardised differences
between groups or conditions, whose scale differs from that of *d*~z~, which is
the mean of a within-participant index divided by its standard deviation.
Nonetheless, being empirically-derived these values remain more representative
of psychology research than the typically used *d* = 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8
[e.g., @cohen1992]. Finally, the *Realistic* estimate from which appropriate
sample size is computed here falls close to the effect size implied by
@schäfer2019's estimate of *r* = 0.16 (translating to *d* &approx;
`r print_d(d_schafer[1L])`) for pre-registered psychology studies.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Effect size for sample size estimation"}
The values in the table above are used by the power analysis to anchor sample
size estimation. Specifically, the *Realistic* scenario *d*~z~ = `r d_real`
serves as the basis for the sample size requirement for detecting the primary
endpoint, i.e., BI~2~ calculated from the first test block. At the necessary sample
size estimated this way, statistical power of the *Best-case* scenario *d*~z~ =
`r d_best` and of the expected BI~3~ effect (*d*~z~ &approx; `r bi3_range`) is
evaluated for informative purposes. Finally, the *Worst-case* *d*~z~ =
`r d_worst` scenario serves to set the rules for group-sequential top-up
sampling if the primary endpoint fails to be detected at the first look when
estimated from a sample size based on the *Realistic* scenario power analysis
(Aim 3, see below).
:::
